definition: The earthy, pleasant scent produced when rain falls on dry soil after a warm, dry spell.
exampleSentence: The first fat drops hit the parched garden and that smell rose up - petrichor, the whole street suddenly breathing again.
etymology: Coined by CSIRO scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas in 'Nature of Argillaceous Odour' (Nature, 7 March 1964) as an 'ichor' or 'tenuous essence derived from rock or stone,' from Greek 'petra' (stone) + 'ichor' (the fluid in the veins of the gods).

definition: The occurrence of happy or beneficial discoveries by accident, plus the wit to notice them.
exampleSentence: She went to the library for a tax form and left with the novel that changed her life - pure serendipity.
etymology: Coined by Horace Walpole in a letter to Horace Mann dated 28 January 1754 - 'a very expressive word' - from the Persian tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip,' whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries.

definition: The warmth of the sun in winter.
exampleSentence: She dragged the kitchen chair onto the icy balcony just to sit in the apricity for ten borrowed minutes.
etymology: From Latin 'apricitas' (warmed by the sun); first recorded in Henry Cockeram's 'English Dictionarie' (1623) as 'the warmenes of the Sunne in winter,' and now obsolete - the same root gave us 'apricot.'

definition: Twilight; the dusk of the evening.
exampleSentence: In the gloaming the hills went violet and the first window lights came on one by one.
etymology: From Old English 'glōmung,' related to 'glōm' (twilight) and to 'glow' - the soft glow that lingers after sunset.

definition: Denoting a past period of idyllic peace and happiness.
exampleSentence: They talked all night about the halcyon summers before everyone scattered across the map.
etymology: From Greek 'halkyon' (kingfisher), a bird the ancients believed calmed the sea while nesting on it at the winter solstice - the 'halcyon days.'

definition: The soft sound of wind whispering through trees.
exampleSentence: They stopped talking just to hear the psithurism move across the poplars.
etymology: From Greek psithuros 'whispering, slanderous' — onomatopoeic, the word breathes like the sound.

definition: The low, distant rumble of thunder.
exampleSentence: All afternoon a brontide rolled along the horizon, but the rain never came.
etymology: From Greek brontē 'thunder'.

definition: A love of night and darkness; finding peace after dark.
exampleSentence: Her nyctophilia kept her up till three, happiest when the house went quiet and black.
etymology: From Greek nyx 'night' + philia 'love'.

definition: Of or occurring in the evening.
exampleSentence: The garden kept vespertine hours — its white flowers opened only at dusk.
etymology: From Latin vesper 'evening'.

definition: The beauty found in imperfection, impermanence, and the worn.
exampleSentence: The cracked, mended bowl was lovelier for the flaw — pure wabi-sabi.
etymology: Japanese wabi 'rustic simplicity' + sabi 'the beauty of age and wear'.

definition: The overwhelming, almost unbearable feeling of cuteness that makes you want to clench your fists and squeeze whatever is so adorable.
exampleSentence: She felt such gigil at the sleeping puppy that she had to bite her own knuckle.
etymology: Borrowed from Tagalog 'gigil'; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in its March 2025 update as both noun and adjective, with the earliest English evidence dated to 1990.

definition: The gap at the base of a hedge made by the regular passage of a small animal.
exampleSentence: A tuft of fur on the bramble showed where a fox slipped nightly through the smeuse.
etymology: Sussex dialect noun, popularised by Robert Macfarlane in 'Landmarks' (2015); related to dialect 'smeuse/smout', to creep through a gap.

definition: The thin film of ice that lacquers leaves, twigs and grass when a freeze follows a partial thaw, making a whole landscape glitter in sunlight.
exampleSentence: Dawn lit the ammil and the hedgerow seemed strung with glass.
etymology: Devon dialect, thought to descend from Old English 'ammel', meaning enamel; recorded by Robert Macfarlane in 'Landmarks'.

definition: The habit of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread.
exampleSentence: His nightstand was a monument to tsundoku, six novels deep and none of them opened.
etymology: Japanese, a Meiji-era pun blending 'tsunde-oku' (to pile up and leave) with 'dokusho' (reading books); the 'oku' was swapped for 'doku' (to read).

definition: The leisurely conversation that lingers at the table after a meal is finished but before anyone gets up.
exampleSentence: Lunch ended at two, but the sobremesa carried us, laughing, well past five.
etymology: Spanish, literally 'over the table', from 'sobre' (over) + 'mesa' (table).

definition: A beer enjoyed outdoors, especially the first one savoured in the open air on a fine day.
exampleSentence: The instant the sun broke through, the whole café spilled onto the pavement for a utepils.
etymology: Norwegian, from 'ute' (outside) + 'pils' (pilsner/lager); added to the Oxford English Dictionary as a loanword filling a lexical gap.

definition: The rumbling, gurgling sound made by gas moving through the intestines.
exampleSentence: In the silent exam hall, his borborygmus was practically a public announcement.
etymology: New Latin, from Greek 'borborygmos', from 'borboryzein' (to rumble) — itself an imitation of the gut's noise.

definition: A queasy, fluttering stomach brought on by nerves; butterflies with an upset edge.
exampleSentence: I had the collywobbles all morning before walking out to give my speech.
etymology: English, dating to around 1823; a 'fanciful formation' (OED) probably reshaping New Latin 'cholera morbus' under the influence of 'colic' and 'wobble'.

definition: A shrewd, utterly unprincipled person, especially a politician who chases office with no regard for party or principle.
exampleSentence: Every election season the airwaves fill with snollygosters promising everything to everyone.
etymology: American English, first known use 1845; probably an alteration of 'snallygaster', a mythical poultry-preying creature of rural Maryland (though that word is attested later, so the link is uncertain).

definition: A habitually smiling face, or the relentlessly cheerful person wearing it.
exampleSentence: Before coffee I can't bear a gigglemug grinning at me across the breakfast table.
etymology: Victorian English slang, recorded in 19th-century dictionaries of slang, combining 'giggle' with 'mug' in its slang sense of 'face'.

definition: Fresh hope; a recovery from despair.
exampleSentence: The first warm morning after a long illness filled her with sudden respair.
etymology: English, with a single Oxford English Dictionary record dated to 1525; the positive counterpart of 'despair', from Latin 'sperare' (to hope).

definition: The restless anticipation of a guest's arrival that keeps sending you to the window or door to check.
exampleSentence: Full of iktsuarpok, she checked the street a dozen times before his car finally turned in.
etymology: From Inuktitut (an Inuit language of the Canadian Arctic), describing the impatient excitement of waiting for someone to come.

definition: The bracing shock felt when first plunging into cold water.
exampleSentence: The curglaff of the loch knocked the breath clean out of me before the swim turned blissful.
etymology: Scots dialect, from 'cur-' (a prefix marking something going awry) + 'glaff' (a sudden blast); recorded in dictionaries of the Scots language.

definition: The pleasure taken in anticipating something before it happens; pre-fun.
exampleSentence: Half the joy of the trip was the voorpret of planning routes and packing the night before.
etymology: Dutch, literally 'pre-fun', from 'voor' (before) + 'pret' (fun, pleasure).

definition: Generous, wholehearted delight in another person's good fortune, with no envy or ulterior motive.
exampleSentence: When she won the prize, his firgun was so genuine it lifted the whole room.
etymology: Modern Hebrew 'firgun', from the verb 'lefargen' (to be generous toward, not to begrudge), itself rooted in Yiddish.

definition: The heavy drowsiness that settles over you just after a large meal.
exampleSentence: Sunday lunch ended in a contented abbiocco, everyone half-asleep on the sofa.
etymology: Italian, of uncertain origin, often linked to the dialect idea of 'going broody like a hen' ('chioccia'); long used in Roman and central Italian speech.

definition: The shimmering, road-like reflection the moon casts across water.
exampleSentence: A silver mångata stretched from the shore to the horizon, as if you could walk to the moon.
etymology: Swedish, from 'måne' (moon) + 'gata' (street, road) — literally 'moon-street'.

definition: Shimmering with a band of shifting lustre, like a cat's eye or polished tiger's-eye stone.
exampleSentence: The silk shifted from green to gold as she moved, chatoyant in the candlelight.
etymology: French, present participle of 'chatoyer' (to shine like a cat's eyes), from 'chat' (cat).

definition: Glowing or flickering softly, with a gentle radiance that plays over a surface without burning.
exampleSentence: Lambent firelight moved across the ceiling as the logs settled.
etymology: From Latin 'lambens', present participle of 'lambere' (to lick); first used in English in the 17th century of flame appearing to 'lick' a surface.

definition: Of grey skies, fog and short sunless days; wintry and misty.
exampleSentence: November settled in, brumous and dim, and the lamps came on by four.
etymology: From French 'brume' (mist, fog), via Latin 'bruma' (winter, the shortest day).

definition: Feeling sick and seedy from too much eating or drinking; hungover.
exampleSentence: He shuffled crapulent into the kitchen, vowing never to mix wines again.
etymology: From Late Latin 'crapulentus', from Latin 'crapula' (intoxication, the after-effects of drink), itself from Greek 'kraipale'.

definition: Pleasantly round and cuddly in build.
exampleSentence: A jolly-timbered uncle in a too-tight waistcoat carved the goose with great ceremony.
etymology: 18th-century English; 'timbered' in the old sense of 'built, framed' (as of a body's frame) softened by 'jolly'.

definition: To gaze longingly and silently at someone who is eating, in the hope of being offered some.
exampleSentence: The dog sat groking at my sandwich with such soulful eyes that I caved.
etymology: Scots dialect (also 'growk'), recorded in the Scottish National Dictionary; of uncertain origin, used of children and dogs begging at the table.

definition: To dash about frantically tidying the house in the short window between learning a guest is coming and their knock at the door.
exampleSentence: Her text gave me ten minutes to scurryfunge before she rang the bell.
etymology: English dialect; from 'scurry' (to rush) with an obscure second element, its sense shifting from 'to scour/scrub' to a hasty tidy-up by the mid-19th century. Still heard in Newfoundland dialect.

definition: To laugh loudly, hard and uncontrollably.
exampleSentence: The whole table began to cachinnate until people at the next booth turned to stare.
etymology: From Latin 'cachinnare' (to laugh aloud), an imitative word echoing the sound of raucous laughter.

definition: To leave abruptly and without ceremony; to make off.
exampleSentence: The moment the bill arrived, he absquatulated to the bathroom and never returned.
etymology: A jocular 19th-century American coinage built on mock-Latin lines, riffing on 'squat' to suggest the opposite of settling down.

definition: To hesitate awkwardly while introducing someone because you've forgotten their name.
exampleSentence: I began to tartle at the party, buying time with 'Of course you two know each other!'
etymology: Scots, recorded in dictionaries of the Scots language; an expressive word for the social stumble of a forgotten name.

definition: The instinctive full-body stretch, often paired with a yawn, that you perform on waking.
exampleSentence: She rose with a luxurious pandiculation, arms flung wide and jaw cracking in a yawn.
etymology: From Latin 'pandiculari' (to stretch oneself), from 'pandere' (to spread, stretch); in English from the 1610s–1640s, first recorded by lexicographer Randle Cotgrave in 1611.

definition: The curved web of space between the outstretched thumb and forefinger.
exampleSentence: He balanced the pencil in the purlicue of his hand while he thought.
etymology: Scots, first recorded 1808 in John Jamieson's dictionary; probably from Scots 'pirlie' (curly, twisted), perhaps via 'pirl' (to twist or spin).

definition: The warm, generous joy you feel at a loved one's happiness with someone else — the opposite of jealousy.
exampleSentence: Instead of envy she felt only compersion as she watched her best friend fall in love.
etymology: Coined by the Kerista commune, a polyamorous community in San Francisco; per the group's records, their 'alphabet board' produced the word on 28 November 1980 as an antonym for jealousy.

definition: A cold sea-fog that rolls in off the North Sea onto the east coast of Scotland and northern England.
exampleSentence: By noon the haar had swallowed the harbour, and the foghorns began their mournful lowing.
etymology: Scots and northern English, recorded from the 17th–18th centuries; probably from Middle Dutch/Low German 'hare' (a biting cold wind), with some influence from Old Norse 'hárr' (hoary, grey).

definition: A person who idly watches activity on a canal — or, more broadly, anyone who stares at length at anything.
exampleSentence: A row of gongoozlers leaned on the lock gates, happily watching the narrowboats rise.
etymology: Canal-workers' slang, first recorded 1904 in H. R. de Salis's 'Bradshaw's Canals', defined as 'an idle and inquisitive person who stands staring'; perhaps from Lincolnshire dialect 'gawn' and 'gooze', both meaning to stare or gape.

definition: A lover of travel and the open road.
exampleSentence: An incurable hodophile, she kept a packed bag by the door year-round.
etymology: From Greek 'hodos' (road, journey) + '-phile' (lover); part of a small family with 'hodophilia' and its antonym 'hodophobia'.

definition: A retired man who passes the time watching construction sites, hands clasped behind his back, offering unasked-for advice.
exampleSentence: Three umarells had gathered at the roadworks by eight, supervising a job no one had asked them to.
etymology: From the Bolognese Emilian 'umarèl' (little man); conceived by writer Danilo Masotti at dawn on 4 February 2005 in Bologna, and admitted to the Italian Zingarelli dictionary in 2021.

definition: Studied carelessness; the art of making something difficult look entirely effortless.
exampleSentence: He wore the tuxedo with such sprezzatura — tie loosened, collar undone — that he looked better than anyone who had tried.
etymology: Italian, coined by Baldassare Castiglione in 'The Book of the Courtier' (1528), from 'sprezzare' (to disdain); literally 'studied carelessness'.

definition: A leisurely stroller who wanders the city to observe and absorb its life.
exampleSentence: He spent the afternoon as a flâneur, drifting through the arcades with no destination in mind.
etymology: From French 'flâner' (to stroll); raised from a pejorative for an idler into an artistic ideal by Charles Baudelaire in the 1860s.

definition: An excessive desire to stay in bed.
exampleSentence: On dark January mornings her clinomania was almost a medical condition.
etymology: From Greek 'kline' (bed) + 'mania' (madness, craving).

definition: A fine, drifting drizzle so light it seems to hang in the air rather than fall.
exampleSentence: A grey smirr hung over the glen, soaking them without ever quite raining.
etymology: Scots, recorded from 1808; origin obscure, perhaps related to Dutch/Low German 'smoren' (to smother, smoke).

definition: A brief glimpse, or a fleeting gleam of light.
exampleSentence: She caught only a glisk of the deer before it melted back into the trees.
etymology: Scots; related to Norwegian dialect 'glisa' (to gleam) and Old English 'glisian' (to glitter), with a frequentative '-k'.

definition: A sudden, violent squall of cold wind sweeping down from a mountainous coast to the sea.
exampleSentence: A williwaw came roaring off the headland and laid the little yacht almost flat.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; a British seamen's word from the mid-19th century, associated with the Strait of Magellan and the Aleutian Islands.

definition: The act or habit of talking in one's sleep.
exampleSentence: His somniloquy was so vivid that she once held a whole conversation with him while he slept.
etymology: From Latin 'somnus' (sleep) + 'loqui' (to speak), modelled on 'soliloquy'; 19th century.

definition: A nosy busybody who must know all the latest gossip.
exampleSentence: The village quidnunc had the news of the engagement before the couple had told their parents.
etymology: From Latin 'quid nunc' (what now?); first used in English in 1709 by Richard Steele in 'The Tatler'.

definition: Of a sound: loud, resonant, and mournful.
exampleSentence: The plangent toll of the buoy bell carried across the dark water.
etymology: From Latin 'plangere' (to strike, beat the breast, lament); early 19th century.

definition: Full of flavour; tasty — and, figuratively, engaging or lively.
exampleSentence: After weeks of bland hospital food, the sapid little stew tasted like a celebration.
etymology: From Latin 'sapidus' (savoury), from 'sapere' (to taste, have flavour); 17th century.

definition: To lie in bed or lounge about long after you should have got up.
exampleSentence: It was a grey Sunday made for nothing but coffee and a long hurkle-durkle.
etymology: Scots rhyming reduplication built on 'hurkle' (to crouch, draw the limbs together); recorded in John Jamieson's dictionary of Scots (Supplement, 1825).

definition: To go out walking in strong wind to clear the head and refresh oneself.
exampleSentence: Stuffy and stuck on the essay, she went to uitwaaien along the blustery sea wall.
etymology: Dutch, from 'uit' (out) + 'waaien' (to blow, of wind); literally 'to blow out'.

definition: A narrow path or alleyway running between two walls or hedges.
exampleSentence: They cut home through a twitten barely wide enough for one.
etymology: Sussex dialect, recorded in W. D. Parish's Dictionary of the Sussex Dialect (1875) and the OED; perhaps related to Old English 'twicen', a place where two roads meet.

definition: Lavish, extravagant spending on food and drink.
exampleSentence: A weekend of oysters and champagne was pure abligurition.
etymology: From Latin 'abligurire' (to squander on delicacies), from 'ab-' (away) + 'ligurire' (to be dainty), from 'lingere' (to lick). Entered English via Nathan Bailey's 1724 dictionary, defined as 'A prodigal spending in Belly-Cheer'.

definition: To wander or roam idly and aimlessly.
exampleSentence: We spent the afternoon stravaiging through the old town.
etymology: Scots, probably an aphetic form of 'extravage', from Medieval Latin 'extravagari' (to wander beyond limits), per the Dictionary of the Scots Language; used by Burns and Hogg.

definition: Spray blown from the crests of waves by a gale; also fine wind-driven snow.
exampleSentence: Spindrift streamed off the breakers in a salt haze.
etymology: Scots formation (c.1600), of uncertain origin; OED links it to 'spoondrift', from 'spoon/spoom' (to sail before the wind) + 'drift'. Popularized in English by novelist William Black (1841–1898).

definition: The bright track of moonlight reflected across water.
exampleSentence: A moonglade lay across the bay like a silver road.
etymology: American English compound of 'moon' + 'glade' (a bright open patch). OED's earliest evidence is 1867, in the writing of James Russell Lowell.

definition: Of or occurring in the dark hours just before dawn.
exampleSentence: They set off in the antelucan hush, before the birds woke.
etymology: From Latin 'antelucanus', from 'ante-' (before) + 'lux, luc-' (light); earliest English use early 17th century.

definition: The fading half-light of dusk; twilight.
exampleSentence: We watched the valley dissolve into the dimpsy.
etymology: West Country (Devon/Somerset) dialect, of uncertain origin; probably from 'dim'. Compare local 'dimmit'/'dumpsey'.

definition: Emerald-green; of or relating to emeralds.
exampleSentence: The lake shone a deep smaragdine under the pines.
etymology: From Latin 'smaragdinus', from Greek 'smaragdos' (emerald); first English use 1382 (Wycliffite Bible).

definition: The strong smell of cooking or burning meat or fat.
exampleSentence: The nidor of the roasting goose filled the house.
etymology: From Latin 'nidor' (a steam, fumes, strong smell), of uncertain origin.

definition: (Of the stomach) to rumble and churn with nausea; to move unsteadily.
exampleSentence: My stomach wambled after the ferry crossing.
etymology: Late Middle English, of uncertain origin; compare Danish 'vamle' (to feel queasy).

definition: A tightrope walker.
exampleSentence: The funambulist crossed between the towers without a net.
etymology: From Latin 'funis' (rope) + 'ambulare' (to walk).

definition: Idle daydreaming; absent-minded indulgence in fancy.
exampleSentence: Caught woolgathering, she missed the question entirely.
etymology: From the literal gathering of stray tufts of wool from hedges — a trivial, wandering errand; figurative sense from the 16th century.

definition: A person who scavenges in river mud at low tide for objects of value.
exampleSentence: The mudlark surfaced with a clay pipe and a Tudor coin.
etymology: From 'mud' + 'lark' (in the sense of a frolic); first recorded 1780s on the Thames.

definition: A foolish, absent-minded or gullible person.
exampleSentence: Don't stand there like a mooncalf — help me lift it.
etymology: From 'moon' + 'calf', from the old belief the moon caused abnormal births; sense 'simpleton' from the 1620s. OED earliest 1565.

definition: An incorrigible, habitual rascal.
exampleSentence: Her youngest was a charming scapegrace who never paid a debt.
etymology: From 'scape' (archaic for 'escape') + 'grace' — literally 'one who has escaped the grace of God'. Merriam-Webster dates first use to 1763; OED's earliest cite is 1809.

definition: A toast to someone's health.
exampleSentence: They raised their glasses with a hearty skoal.
etymology: From Danish/Norwegian/Swedish 'skål' (a toast), literally 'bowl, cup', from Old Norse 'skál'; in English from c.1600.

definition: To rain in very fine, misty drops.
exampleSentence: It mizzled all morning, too soft to call rain.
etymology: Late Middle English 'misellen', of obscure origin; compare Dutch dialect 'miezelen' (to drizzle).

definition: The rosy glow on mountain summits just before sunrise or after sunset.
exampleSentence: The peaks burned pink with alpenglow as the sun dropped.
etymology: Partial calque of German 'Alpenglühen' (Alpen 'Alps' + Glühen 'glow'); OED's earliest evidence is 1862, in a letter by W. H. Brewer.

definition: A soft, gentle breeze, especially from the west.
exampleSentence: A zephyr stirred the curtains on the warm afternoon.
etymology: From Latin 'Zephyrus', from Greek 'Zephyros', the personified west wind; 'gentle breeze' sense c.1600.

definition: To look amorously or longingly at someone.
exampleSentence: He smickered at her across the crowded room.
etymology: Scots and dialect English; related to obsolete 'smicker' meaning elegant, amorous.

definition: The traditional collective noun for a flight of larks.
exampleSentence: An exaltation of larks rose singing from the meadow.
etymology: From Latin 'exaltare' (to raise high); the bird sense is listed in the Book of St Albans (1486) as 'an Exaltynge of larkys'.

definition: A great wheeling flock of starlings; a low murmuring sound.
exampleSentence: A murmuration of starlings rippled across the dusk sky.
etymology: From Latin 'murmurare' (to murmur); the starling-flock sense recorded among the collective nouns of the late medieval period.

definition: The dappled, shifting sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees.
exampleSentence: We lay on the moss and watched the komorebi tremble gold across our hands.
etymology: Japanese 木漏れ日, from 木 'ko' (tree) + 漏れ 'more' (leaking through) + 日 'bi' (sunlight); literally 'sunlight that leaks through trees'.

definition: The shimmering trail of moonlight or other light reflected on water at night.
exampleSentence: From the ferry we watched the yakamoz stretch like spilled silver toward the city.
etymology: Turkish, ultimately from Greek; once also the phosphorescence of sea plankton, now chiefly the glitter of moonlight on water.

definition: An unhurried coffee-and-pastry break taken with others purely for the pleasure of pausing together.
exampleSentence: The whole office stops at three for fika, and no one dares schedule a meeting over it.
etymology: Swedish, a playful back-slang reversal of the old word 'kaffi' (coffee); the social ritual around the cup, not just the drink.

definition: The act of tenderly running your fingers through the hair of someone you love.
exampleSentence: She fell asleep mid-sentence as he gave her slow cafuné on the sofa.
etymology: Brazilian Portuguese, of African (likely Bantu) origin carried into Brazil; an everyday gesture of tenderness with no English equivalent.

definition: The excess weight gained from comfort-eating one's way through grief or stress.
exampleSentence: Three months of breakup ice cream left him with a soft layer of kummerspeck.
etymology: German, from 'Kummer' (grief) + 'Speck' (bacon, fat); literally 'grief bacon'. Recorded in the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: The perfect, witty comeback that arrives only after the moment to use it has passed.
exampleSentence: Halfway down the stairs the devastating treppenwitz finally came to her, far too late.
etymology: German, from 'Treppe' (stairs) + 'Witz' (joke); a 'staircase joke', calquing the French 'esprit de l'escalier'. In the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: The seemingly malicious behaviour of inanimate objects that conspire to thwart us.
exampleSentence: The printer jamming five minutes before the deadline was pure resistentialism.
etymology: Coined in 1948 by humorist Paul Jennings in 'Report on Resistentialism' (The Spectator); a blend of Latin 'res' (thing) + French 'résister' + 'existentialism', spoofing Sartre. Slogan: 'Les choses sont contre nous'.

definition: A face so smug or irritating that it seems to be begging for a slap.
exampleSentence: The contestant's gloating smirk was a textbook backpfeifengesicht.
etymology: German, from 'Backpfeife' (a slap on the cheek) + 'Gesicht' (face); literally 'a face that needs slapping'.

definition: The involuntary cinema of the mind that plays out vivid imagined scenes.
exampleSentence: One unread text and her kopfkino was already screening three disaster sequels.
etymology: German, from 'Kopf' (head) + 'Kino' (cinema); literally 'head cinema'.

definition: The dispiriting state of looking worse after a haircut than you did before it.
exampleSentence: He left the barber's in full age-otori, hat jammed low over his ears.
etymology: Japanese 上げ劣り, from 'age' (to cut/raise) + 'otori' (inferior); coming out looking inferior to before.

definition: A joke so clumsily told and unfunny that you cannot help laughing anyway.
exampleSentence: His pun was such a jayus that the whole table groaned and then cracked up.
etymology: Indonesian slang; a joke whose comedic value comes precisely from its spectacular failure to be funny.

definition: Weather that looks beautiful through the window but is miserable to be out in.
exampleSentence: Bright sun, bitter wind — classic gluggaveður, so we stayed in with cocoa.
etymology: Icelandic, from 'gluggi' (window) + 'veður' (weather); literally 'window-weather'.

definition: A person who turns up to mourn at a wake mainly for the free refreshments.
exampleSentence: Every funeral in town drew the same pesamenteiro, weeping near the buffet.
etymology: Portuguese, from 'pêsames' (condolences) + the agentive suffix '-eiro'; one who 'does condolences', chiefly for the food.

definition: The damp ring a cold, sweating glass leaves behind on a table.
exampleSentence: Three culaccini overlapped on the wood where our drinks had stood all afternoon.
etymology: Italian, a diminutive based on 'culaccio'; the little mark left by the bottom of a wet glass.

definition: The rush of joy felt on reuniting with someone after a long time apart.
exampleSentence: The airport arrivals hall was a sea of tearful retrouvailles and crushed bouquets.
etymology: French, from 'retrouver' (to find again); literally 'rediscoveries', the happiness of meeting again.

definition: The quiet certainty, on first meeting someone, that the two of you will fall in love.
exampleSentence: It wasn't love at first sight, just koi no yokan — a sense of what was coming.
etymology: Japanese 恋の予感, from 'koi' (love) + 'no' (of) + 'yokan' (premonition); the premonition of love rather than love itself.

definition: The fluttering tangle of nerves and excitement just before a journey begins.
exampleSentence: The night before the flight she lay awake, heart drumming with resfeber.
etymology: Swedish, from 'resa' (journey) + 'feber' (fever); the 'travel-fever' of anticipation and anxiety combined.

definition: A gullible person who will credulously swallow whatever they are told.
exampleSentence: Every conspiracy thread found a fresh gobemouche ready to believe and repost it.
etymology: French, from 'gober' (to gulp down) + 'mouche' (fly); literally a 'fly-swallower', mouth hanging open. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Stoic inner grit that keeps you going long after reason says to quit.
exampleSentence: It took pure sisu to finish the marathon on a sprained ankle in the sleet.
etymology: Finnish, from 'sisus' (the insides, the gut); a near-mythic Finnish ideal of resolve in adversity.

definition: The intuitive art of reading a room and sensing others' unspoken moods.
exampleSentence: She had the nunchi to change the subject the instant the table went quiet.
etymology: Korean 눈치, from 'nun' (eye); literally 'eye-measure', the quick gauging of a situation through subtle cues.

definition: A cosy, low-key Friday night spent unwinding at home with snacks and loved ones.
exampleSentence: Blankets, tacos and a film: their fredagsmys was sacred after a long week.
etymology: Swedish, from 'fredag' (Friday) + 'mys' (cosiness); first appearing in Swedish print in 1994 and entering the SAOL dictionary in 2006.

definition: The giddy, fluttering thrill of a romantic or exciting moment.
exampleSentence: Just remembering his text gave her a fresh wave of kilig.
etymology: Tagalog; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in March 2016, its earliest cited use being 1981 in the Diliman Review.

definition: Looking attractive only from a distance, the appeal evaporating up close.
exampleSentence: From across the bar he seemed striking, but it turned out he was purely layogenic.
etymology: Philippine English, from Tagalog 'layo' (distance) + the suffix '-genic' (as in photogenic); good-looking at a remove.

definition: Unusually and constantly sensitive to the cold.
exampleSentence: So friolero was she that she wore wool socks indoors through June.
etymology: Spanish, from 'frío' (cold) + the suffix '-ero'; describing a person who feels the cold acutely. Recorded by the Real Academia Española.

definition: Floating in the giddy euphoria of beginning to fall in love.
exampleSentence: He grinned at his phone all morning, hopelessly forelsket.
etymology: Norwegian and Danish, the past participle of 'forelske seg' (to fall in love); the intoxicating first rush of new love.

definition: Warmly friendly, kindly and snugly comfortable, of a person or place.
exampleSentence: The wee couthie pub welcomed us in from the rain with a roaring fire.
etymology: Scots, from 'couth' (known, familiar, kindly); the opposite of the now-common 'uncouth'. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: To do nothing on purpose, idling without aim or guilt.
exampleSentence: On Sundays she simply niksens by the window, watching the street go by.
etymology: Dutch, from 'niks' (nothing); the deliberate, restorative practice of doing nothing at all.

definition: To scratch your head in the hope of jogging loose a forgotten memory.
exampleSentence: He stood in the doorway to pana po'o, trying to recall why he'd come in.
etymology: Hawaiian; literally to scratch the head ('po'o') to help retrieve something forgotten.

definition: To walk on tiptoe across sand or ground too hot to bear underfoot.
exampleSentence: We had to hanyauku the last stretch of beach to reach the cool of the water.
etymology: Rukwangali, of Namibia; recorded in the 1994 Bukenkango Rukwangali–English dictionary (Kloppers & Bredell).

definition: The act of rising at dawn and going outside expressly to hear the first birdsong of the morning.
exampleSentence: We set an alarm for four and slipped into the garden for a gökotta before anyone else woke.
etymology: Swedish, from 'gök' (cuckoo) + 'otta' (the early hours before dawn, from Old Norse 'ótta'); a tradition linked to Ascension Day, documented in The Local's guide to Swedish life.

definition: Affectionate, wordless sulking meant to signal hurt feelings and quietly invite the other person to make amends.
exampleSentence: She wasn't truly angry, just in a bit of tampo, waiting for him to notice and coax her back.
etymology: Tagalog 'tampó', a noun from the root meaning to withdraw warmth when hurt; recorded in Tagalog dictionaries as 'sulking; silent treatment; grievance'.

definition: A gift or treat a traveller brings home specifically to share their trip with family and friends.
exampleSentence: He never returned from a work trip without dried mangoes as pasalubong for the whole office.
etymology: Tagalog 'pasalubong', literally 'something for the welcoming', from 'pa-' + 'salubong' (to meet, to welcome); entered the OED with earliest evidence from 1933 in Philippine Magazine.

definition: The glowing pride and joy you feel at the achievements of someone you love, especially a child.
exampleSentence: Watching her daughter conduct the orchestra, she felt a wave of naches she could barely contain.
etymology: Yiddish 'nakhes', from Hebrew 'naḥath' (contentment); listed in Merriam-Webster and the OED among naturalized Yiddish borrowings.

definition: A sudden brief shiver of excitement or thrill that ripples through you.
exampleSentence: When the choir hit the final chord, a frisson ran straight up the back of her neck.
etymology: French for 'shiver', from Late Latin 'friction-, frictio', taken as a derivative of 'frigēre' (to be cold); defined by Merriam-Webster as 'a sudden strong feeling of excitement or fear'.

definition: A sudden, overwhelming jolt of love at first sight.
exampleSentence: They met for ten minutes at a wedding, and for him it was an undeniable coup de foudre.
etymology: French, literally 'stroke of lightning'; Merriam-Webster defines it as 'an astonishing occurrence; especially: overwhelming love at first sight'.

definition: A person whose unconventional, even plain features add up to a striking and magnetic beauty.
exampleSentence: Photographers adored her as a jolie laide, all crooked nose and unforgettable, arresting face.
etymology: French, literally 'pretty-ugly', from 'jolie' (pretty) + 'laide' (ugly); Merriam-Webster glosses it as a woman 'attractive though not conventionally pretty'.

definition: Deliberately performed cuteness — a coy, charming display of adorableness to win affection.
exampleSentence: He dropped his voice into exaggerated aegyo to wheedle the last dumpling off her plate.
etymology: Korean; added to the OED in its September 2021 Korean-wave update, defined as a charm or cuteness considered characteristic of Korean popular culture (compare Japanese 'kawaii').

definition: A livestream or video in which the host eats a huge quantity of food while chatting to viewers.
exampleSentence: She unwound after exams by watching a noodle mukbang, oddly soothed by the slurping and gossip.
etymology: Korean blend of 'meokda' (to eat) + 'bangsong' (broadcast); per the OED, its earliest evidence is from 2013, added in the September 2021 Korean update.

definition: Closeness built through affectionate physical touch, as between parent and child or close friends.
exampleSentence: Plenty of hugs and hand-holding meant the team's skinship made their reunions genuinely warm.
etymology: A blend of English 'skin' + 'kinship', modelled on Korean 'seukinsip' and earlier Japanese 'sukinshippu'; added to the OED in September 2021.

definition: The unhurried, open-air life — spending regular time outdoors as an essential part of wellbeing.
exampleSentence: Rain or shine, their weekends were devoted to friluftsliv: walking, foraging, and coffee by a fire.
etymology: Norwegian, 'fri' (free) + 'luft' (air) + 'liv' (life); coined by playwright Henrik Ibsen in his 1859 poem 'Paa Vidderne' (On the Heights).

definition: The rising panic that life's chances are closing and time is running out to seize them.
exampleSentence: As her fortieth birthday neared, a Torschlusspanik pushed her to finally start the business.
etymology: German, 'Tor' (gate) + 'Schluss' (closing) + 'Panik' (panic); from medieval city gates locking at dusk, defined in the Duden and applied to life decisions.

definition: A dreamy daze or trance in which you drift far from what is in front of you.
exampleSentence: He stared out at the rain and slid into a dwam, missing his name being called twice.
etymology: Scots, related to Old English 'dwolma' (chaos, confusion) and Old Saxon 'dwalm' (delusion); attested from the 16th century in the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: A noisy uproar, squabble, or general commotion.
exampleSentence: A burst pipe at midnight set off a glorious stramash of buckets, shouting, and slamming doors.
etymology: Scots, of uncertain origin; recorded in the Dictionaries of the Scots Language from 1803 meaning 'an uproar, commotion, hubbub'.

definition: A person dogged by chronic bad luck, the one the spilled soup always lands on.
exampleSentence: Poor schlimazel — he finally bought an umbrella, and that was the week of the drought.
etymology: Yiddish 'shlimazl', from Middle High German 'slim' (crooked) + Hebrew 'mazzāl' (luck); in Merriam-Webster, contrasted with the bungling 'schlemiel'.

definition: A snatch of music that lodges in your head and replays itself against your will.
exampleSentence: One advert jingle became such an earworm that she hummed it absent-mindedly for three days.
etymology: A 1980s loan-translation of German 'Ohrwurm' ('ear' + 'worm'); defined by Merriam-Webster as 'a song or melody that keeps repeating in one's mind'.

definition: The blissful, guilt-free sweetness of pleasant idleness.
exampleSentence: After the harvest they surrendered to dolce far niente, sprawled in the shade doing absolutely nothing.
etymology: Italian, literally 'sweet doing nothing'; Merriam-Webster records its first English use in 1814, glossing it as 'pleasant relaxation in carefree idleness'.

definition: A hug that wraps you in warmth and safety; also a snug little cubbyhole.
exampleSentence: After the bad news she just wanted a long cwtch from her mam and nothing more.
etymology: Welsh, thought to derive from Old French 'couche' (a resting or hiding place); listed in Collins meaning both a cuddle and a cubbyhole.

definition: The warm, cosy, good-natured cheer of a snug and friendly gathering.
exampleSentence: Candlelight, mulled wine, and old friends gave the little cabin an unmistakable gemütlichkeit.
etymology: German, from 'gemütlich' (cosy, agreeable), from 'Gemüt' (mind, heart); Merriam-Webster defines it as 'cordiality, friendliness'.

definition: Pompous, wordy language so tangled it becomes unintelligible.
exampleSentence: The contract was forty pages of legal gobbledygook nobody on the team could actually parse.
etymology: Coined by US Congressman Maury Maverick in a memo of 30 March 1944 banning the bureaucratic style; he said it evoked a turkey's pompous 'gobble'. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A charming, amusing first encounter that sparks a future romance.
exampleSentence: They had a perfect meet-cute, both reaching for the last copy of the same battered paperback.
etymology: From the screenwriting phrase 'to meet cute', familiar in Hollywood by 1941; the OED and Merriam-Webster record the noun from 1952.

definition: To swell with delighted pride, especially over someone you love.
exampleSentence: Grandpa couldn't stop kvelling when the baby took her first wobbling steps across the kitchen.
etymology: Yiddish 'kveln' (to be delighted), from Middle High German 'quellen' (to well or gush); in Merriam-Webster, with earliest English print evidence from 1952.

definition: To spruce something up with a small, finishing tweak that completes the look.
exampleSentence: She zhuzhed the plain table with a runner and a jug of wildflowers before the guests arrived.
etymology: An imitative word popularised in styling and drag culture; added by Merriam-Webster on 27 September 2023 in a batch of 690 new words, defined as a small improvement that completes the overall look.

definition: To snuggle in close and cosy, nestling against someone or something warm.
exampleSentence: On stormy nights the children would coorie into the big armchair under one shared blanket.
etymology: Scots, a diminutive of 'coor' (to cower or crouch); recorded in the Dictionaries of the Scots Language and in Collins as 'to nestle or snuggle'.

definition: To cheat or hoodwink someone with a brazen bit of trickery.
exampleSentence: The smooth salesman tried to hornswoggle them into buying a roof they plainly didn't need.
etymology: A fanciful American coinage of obscure origin, dating to about 1829; defined in Merriam-Webster as 'to deceive' or 'bamboozle'.

definition: To understand something so deeply and intuitively that you seem to merge with it.
exampleSentence: It took weeks before she truly grokked the new system rather than just following the steps.
etymology: Coined by Robert A. Heinlein in his 1961 novel 'Stranger in a Strange Land' as a Martian word literally meaning 'to drink'; in Merriam-Webster and the OED.

definition: So choked up with emotion that you can barely speak.
exampleSentence: Reading her late father's letter aloud, she got too verklempt to finish the final line.
etymology: Yiddish 'farklemt' (depressed, gripped), from a Germanic root meaning 'to press or squeeze'; popularised by a 1990s sketch-comedy character and listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Looking pale, wan, and a bit off-colour.
exampleSentence: You're awful peely-wally this morning — away back to bed and I'll bring soup.
etymology: Scots, a reduplicated form linked to 'pale' and the sickly sense of 'peelie' (attested 1808); in Collins and the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Ridiculous, implausible, and not to be taken seriously.
exampleSentence: He had some cockamamie scheme to get rich selling ice to penguins.
etymology: American English, attested by 1946; probably an alteration of 'decalcomania' via the children's transfer-tattoos once called 'cockamamies'. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Glowingly pleased and delighted with how something has turned out.
exampleSentence: She was dead chuffed when her little garden won a ribbon at the village show.
etymology: British informal, from dialectal 'chuff' (pleased, puffed up with pride); defined in Collins as very pleased.

definition: Utterly astonished, as if struck speechless in the mouth.
exampleSentence: We were gobsmacked when the quiet kid from the back row won the national prize.
etymology: British, from 'gob' (slang for mouth, of Celtic origin) + 'smacked'; in Collins and the OED, with an earliest citation from 1935.

definition: Irritable and short-tempered as a direct result of being hungry.
exampleSentence: Feed him before the meeting or he'll get hangry and snap at the whole room.
etymology: A portmanteau of 'hungry' and 'angry'; added to Merriam-Webster in September 2018, defined as 'irritable or angry because of hunger'.

definition: Set askew or diagonally; out of true alignment.
exampleSentence: The earthquake left every picture in the hall hanging cattywampus.
etymology: 19th-century American English of uncertain origin, probably from 'cater' (diagonal, from French 'quatre') plus a fanciful element; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: In hopeless, jumbled disorder.
exampleSentence: The books were stacked higgledy-piggledy, fiction and physics toppling into one another.
etymology: A 16th-century rhyming reduplication, probably alluding to the jostling of pigs huddling together; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Strongly smelling of something; evocative of a fragrance.
exampleSentence: The kitchen was redolent of cinnamon and cloves.
etymology: From Latin 'redolere' to emit a scent.

definition: The state of being infatuated and obsessively preoccupied with another person.
exampleSentence: His limerence faded once the relationship became routine.
etymology: Coined in the 1970s by psychologist Dorothy Tennov.

definition: A state of listlessness and spiritual apathy; torpor of the soul.
exampleSentence: A profound acedia kept him from any meaningful work.
etymology: From Greek 'akedia' meaning lack of care.

definition: A state of serene calmness and freedom from emotional disturbance.
exampleSentence: The philosopher sought ataraxia through detachment.
etymology: From Greek 'ataraxia' meaning impassiveness, calm.

definition: A soft murmuring or rustling sound; a whisper.
exampleSentence: A susurrus of leaves filled the quiet wood.
etymology: From Latin 'susurrus' meaning a humming, whisper.

definition: Something that brings a final end or release; a settling.
exampleSentence: The scandal put the quietus on his political career.
etymology: From Latin 'quietus est' meaning he is quit, discharged.

definition: The act of throwing someone or something out of a window; by extension, a swift removal from power.
exampleSentence: The board meeting ended in a quiet defenestration: by Friday the founder's name was already gone from the door.
etymology: From Latin 'de-' (down from) + 'fenestra' (window); coined around the Second Defenestration of Prague (23 May 1618), when Protestant nobles threw two regents ~70 feet from a castle window, sparking the Thirty Years' War.

definition: A misheard word or phrase, especially in a song, that yields a new meaning.
exampleSentence: For years he belted 'wrapped up like a douche' into his hairbrush - a mondegreen he refused to give up even after learning the real line.
etymology: Coined by Sylvia Wright in 'The Death of Lady Mondegreen' (Harper's, November 1954), after she misheard the ballad line 'laid him on the green' as 'Lady Mondegreen.'

definition: The realization that each random passer-by is living a life as vivid and complex as your own.
exampleSentence: Stuck in traffic, watching a hundred lit windows, she felt that vertigo of sonder - every one of them a whole novel.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows' (2012), adapted from French 'sonder' (to probe) and German 'sonder' (special).

definition: A sudden, joyous turn for the good at the darkest point of a story.
exampleSentence: Right when the city seemed lost, the horns sounded on the hill - a perfect eucatastrophe.
etymology: Coined by J. R. R. Tolkien (from a 1939 St Andrews lecture, published 1947 in 'Essays Presented to Charles Williams'): 'Since we do not appear to possess a word... I will call it Eucatastrophe,' from Greek 'eu-' (good) + 'catastrophe' (sudden turn).

definition: The scented trail left lingering in the air after a perfumed person passes.
exampleSentence: She had already turned the corner, but her sillage hung in the stairwell like a signature.
etymology: From French 'sillage' (the wake of a ship), from 'sillon' (furrow), ultimately from Latin 'secare' (to cut).

definition: Glittering with gold or tinsel; showily brilliant.
exampleSentence: The ballroom was clinquant with chandeliers, every surface throwing back light.
etymology: From French 'clinquant,' present participle of the obsolete 'clinquer' (to clink, glitter), of imitative origin.

definition: A deep, wistful longing for a home or past that may never have existed; bittersweet homesickness for the irrecoverable.
exampleSentence: Hearing the old language on the train platform filled her with hiraeth for a village she had never actually lived in.
etymology: A Welsh word with no exact English equivalent, blending grief and longing for the lost or the never-was.

definition: A wish or inclination so slight it prompts no action whatsoever.
exampleSentence: He had a velleity to learn the cello - enough to admire one in a shop window, never enough to buy it.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'velleitas,' from Latin 'velle' (to wish, to will).

definition: Of or resembling twilight; (of animals) active mainly at dawn and dusk.
exampleSentence: Deer are crepuscular, so the meadow filled with them only as the light began to fail.
etymology: From Latin 'crepusculum' (twilight), from 'creper' (dusky, obscure).

definition: Feeling the presence of something holy, awe-inspiring and beyond comprehension.
exampleSentence: Standing alone in the vast empty cathedral, she felt something numinous she had no church for.
etymology: From Latin 'numen' (divine will, the nod of a god); given its modern sense by theologian Rudolf Otto in 1917.

definition: A wistful nostalgia for a time you never experienced yourself.
exampleSentence: Flipping through the stranger's 1970s photo album, he was ambushed by anemoia for a decade he never lived.
etymology: Coined by John Koenig in 'The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows,' from Greek 'anemos' (wind) + 'nous' (mind).

definition: The lingering ringing or jingling of bells.
exampleSentence: The whole valley filled with the tintinnabulation of the morning bells.
etymology: From Latin tintinnabulum 'bell'; popularized by Edgar Allan Poe's poem 'The Bells' (1849).

definition: Occupying a threshold; in between two states or stages.
exampleSentence: Airports at 3 a.m. have a liminal feel — nowhere, between everywhere.
etymology: From Latin limen 'threshold'.

definition: Deep human flourishing; happiness as a whole life lived well.
exampleSentence: For Aristotle, pleasure was fleeting but eudaimonia was the point of a life.
etymology: From Greek eu 'good' + daimōn 'guiding spirit'; Aristotle's name for the highest human good.

definition: Unfamiliar and strange, yet marvellous.
exampleSentence: The first snow felt selcouth to the desert child — alien and wonderful at once.
etymology: From Old English seldcūth, from seldan 'seldom' + cūth 'known'.

definition: A surge of soul, passion, and authenticity in art or performance.
exampleSentence: Her voice cracked on the last note, and that was the duende — raw and alive.
etymology: Spanish duende 'goblin, spirit'; elevated by Federico García Lorca in a 1933 lecture to mean art's dark, vital magic.

definition: A wave-smashed chasm or fissure cut into a sea-cliff.
exampleSentence: The path skirted a zawn where the Atlantic boomed forty feet below.
etymology: Cornish dialect, from Cornish 'sawan' (chasm, gully); recorded in Robert Macfarlane's glossary of landscape terms.

definition: A place where one feels safe, at home and from which one draws strength; one's deepest refuge.
exampleSentence: The old reading chair by the window was her querencia after a brutal week.
etymology: Spanish, from 'querer' (to want, to love) and ultimately Latin 'quaerere' (to seek); originally the part of the bullring a bull claims for its stand. Entered English via Hemingway's 'Death in the Afternoon' (1932).

definition: A person skilled in the art of dinner-table conversation; a brilliant talker over a meal.
exampleSentence: A natural deipnosophist, she could turn a dull supper into the night's best entertainment.
etymology: From Greek 'deipnon' (dinner) + 'sophistes' (master of a craft); from Athenaeus's c. 3rd-century work 'Deipnosophistai', in which learned men converse at a banquet.

definition: A habitual faultfinder who can sour any experience with discontent.
exampleSentence: Travel with a smelfungus and even the Alps will somehow be too cold, too steep and overrated.
etymology: Coined (as 'Smelfungus') by Laurence Sterne in 'A Sentimental Journey' (1768) to mock the relentlessly critical travel writer Tobias Smollett.

definition: A person who stubbornly clings to a habit or belief even after being shown it is wrong; also, the mistaken notion itself.
exampleSentence: He's a mumpsimus about the apostrophe and will defend his error to the grave.
etymology: From a tale of an illiterate priest who kept saying Latin 'mumpsimus' for 'sumpsimus' ('we have taken') and refused to be corrected; in English use since the 16th century.

definition: The anxious wakefulness in the small hours before dawn, when worries swell out of all proportion.
exampleSentence: At four in the morning, deep in uhtceare, every small problem felt like a catastrophe.
etymology: Old English, from 'uht(a)' (the restless hour before dawn) + 'cearu' (care, sorrow); found in Old English poetry such as 'The Wife's Lament'.

definition: A love of solitude and a longing to withdraw from other people.
exampleSentence: After the week-long conference, a wave of apanthropy sent her gladly home to silence.
etymology: 18th-century English, from Greek 'apo-' (away from) + 'anthropos' (human being).

definition: A wordless, charged look shared by two people who both want to begin something but each waits for the other to start.
exampleSentence: Across the table passed a long mamihlapinatapai before either dared to mention the kiss.
etymology: From the Yaghan language of Tierra del Fuego; the 1994 Guinness Book of World Records lists it as the 'most succinct word', glossed as looking at each other hoping the other will offer to do what both desire but neither will begin.

definition: The bowl-shaped hollow formed by cupping both hands together; a double handful.
exampleSentence: He scooped a gowpen of spring water and drank straight from his hands.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, from Old Norse 'gaupn' (the cupped hands forming a hollow); attested in Older Scots from the late 15th century and in Merriam-Webster's unabridged dictionary.

definition: The whirring sound made by a covey of partridges bursting into flight.
exampleSentence: A sudden zwer from the stubble field marked where the birds had been hiding.
etymology: Exmoor dialect, an onomatopoeic term recorded in Robert Macfarlane's glossaries of nature words.

definition: A puppet on strings; figuratively, a politician whose actions are controlled by someone pulling the strings behind them.
exampleSentence: Voters grew tired of electing quockerwodgers who answered only to their donors.
etymology: 19th-century English; originally a wooden toy figure jerked by strings, later applied derisively to a politician acting at another's command.

definition: Having the soft, pearly iridescence of mother-of-pearl.
exampleSentence: At dawn the clouds turned nacreous, faintly pink and blue like the inside of a shell.
etymology: From 'nacre' (mother-of-pearl), via French from Italian 'nacchera', ultimately of Arabic origin, + the suffix '-ous'.

definition: Of or relating to yesterday or to a former time.
exampleSentence: He woke with a pridian headache, the lingering toll of the night before.
etymology: From Latin 'pridianus', from 'pridie' (on the day before).

definition: Warmly cosy and convivial; the snug pleasure of good company in a comfortable place.
exampleSentence: The little café was so gezellig that we stayed three hours longer than we'd meant to.
etymology: Dutch, from 'gezel' (companion, friend), related to the idea of togetherness; cognate in feeling to German 'gemütlich'.

definition: Having beautifully shaped buttocks.
exampleSentence: The sculptor was famed for his callipygian marble nymphs.
etymology: Dated to 1800; Latinised from Greek 'kallipygos' (the name of a statue of Aphrodite), from 'kalli-/kallos' (beauty) + 'pyge' (buttocks).

definition: Wandering alone; given to solitary roaming.
exampleSentence: She spent a solivagant summer crossing the hills with nothing but a pack and a map.
etymology: From Latin 'solus' (alone) + 'vagari' (to wander).

definition: Aiming at peace; conciliatory and inclined to smooth over conflict.
exampleSentence: Her irenic tone calmed the meeting just as it threatened to boil over.
etymology: From Greek 'eirenikos' (peaceful), from 'eirene' (peace).

definition: Of, relating to, or happening in the morning; active at dawn.
exampleSentence: His matutinal routine of coffee and birdsong was sacred and unhurried.
etymology: From Late Latin 'matutinalis', from Latin 'matutinus' (of the morning), linked to Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn.

definition: To give off flashing, glittering points of light; to sparkle.
exampleSentence: Frost made the whole meadow coruscate as the sun cleared the hedge.
etymology: From Latin 'coruscare' (to flash, glitter, vibrate).

definition: In a direction contrary to the sun's course; counterclockwise, traditionally regarded as unlucky.
exampleSentence: Folklore warned against walking widdershins around the old church.
etymology: From Middle Low German 'weddersinnes' (against the way), from 'wider' (against) + 'sin' (direction); naturalised into Scots and English.

definition: In the direction of the sun's apparent course; clockwise, traditionally regarded as auspicious.
exampleSentence: For luck, the bride was led deasil three times around the hearth.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic 'deiseil', related to 'deas' (right hand, south); the sunwise turn for good fortune.

definition: Early; in good time, before it is too late.
exampleSentence: We rose betimes to catch the tide while the harbour was still grey.
etymology: Middle English 'bitimes', from 'by' + 'time' + adverbial '-s'; in literary use since the 14th century.

definition: Perhaps; possibly; maybe.
exampleSentence: Aiblins he'll come round by spring, once the worst of his temper's cooled.
etymology: Scots, from 'able' + '-ins' (an adverbial suffix); literally 'ably', shading into 'possibly'. Familiar from the poems of Robert Burns.

definition: Freshly melted snow; very cold, half-thawed slush.
exampleSentence: The mountain stream ran with snowbroth, numbing his hands within seconds.
etymology: From Old English 'snāw' (snow) + 'broth'; in English from c.1600. Shakespeare uses it in 'Measure for Measure' (I.4), where Lucio calls Angelo 'a man whose blood is very snow-broth'.

definition: A person who begins to learn or study only late in life.
exampleSentence: A proud opsimath, he took up Greek and the cello in his seventies.
etymology: From Greek 'opse' (late) + 'manthanein' (to learn); in English from the 1650s.

definition: The Finnish practice of getting pleasantly drunk at home in your underwear with no intention of going out.
exampleSentence: After the brutal week, his only weekend plan was a determined session of kalsarikännit.
etymology: Finnish, from 'kalsari' (underpants) + 'känni' (drunkenness); anglicised as 'pantsdrunk'. The popular 'no intention of going out' gloss comes from Finland's own promotional emoji set (2015).

definition: The worship of words.
exampleSentence: His epeolatry was incurable: he read the dictionary for pleasure and hoarded rare adjectives.
etymology: From Greek 'epos' (word) + '-latry' (worship); coined by Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. in 'The Professor at the Breakfast-Table' (Atlantic essays from 1859, collected as a book in 1860).

definition: Soft hail — the small white snow pellets formed when supercooled droplets freeze onto a falling snowflake.
exampleSentence: Graupel pattered against the tent like spilled rice before the real snow began.
etymology: From German 'Graupel', a diminutive of 'Graupe' (pearl barley, groats).

definition: A standing wave that sloshes slowly back and forth in an enclosed body of water such as a lake or harbour.
exampleSentence: After the earthquake a gentle seiche rocked the harbour for hours, lifting and dropping the moored boats.
etymology: Swiss French, of obscure origin; promoted as a scientific term by the hydrologist François-Alphonse Forel for the oscillations of Lake Geneva in 1890.

definition: The shrill chirping made by crickets and other insects rubbing body parts together.
exampleSentence: The summer dusk filled with the stridulation of a thousand crickets.
etymology: From French 'striduler', from Latin 'stridulus' (shrill, creaking), from 'stridere' (to creak).

definition: Greediness; an excessive, gluttonous appetite.
exampleSentence: He attacked the buffet with a gulosity that emptied three platters before the toast was finished.
etymology: From Late Latin 'gulositas', from Latin 'gulosus' (gluttonous), from 'gula' (throat, gullet); in English before 1500.

definition: Careless, illegible handwriting; a crude scrawl.
exampleSentence: The prescription was the usual medical griffonage, unreadable to everyone but the pharmacist.
etymology: From French 'griffonnage', from 'griffonner' (to scribble), ultimately from 'griffe' (claw).

definition: A person obsessively anxious about their own health, forever fearing illness.
exampleSentence: A lifelong valetudinarian, he travelled with a suitcase of remedies for ailments he did not have.
etymology: From Latin 'valetudinarius' (sickly), from 'valetudo' (state of health), from 'valere' (to be well); early 18th century.

definition: A neighbour whose house is on fire.
exampleSentence: Smoke pouring next door, he ran out shouting that he had become, of all things, a ucalegon's neighbour.
etymology: From Ucalegon, a Trojan elder whose house burned in the sack of the city (Virgil, 'Aeneid' 2.311–312, 'iam proximus ardet Ucalegon'); recorded as an English noun in Webster's New International Dictionary (1934).

definition: A noisy quarrel, brawl, or uproar.
exampleSentence: The council meeting collapsed into a full collieshangie over the parking scheme.
etymology: Scots, recorded from 1737; origin uncertain, perhaps from Gaelic 'coileid' (hubbub) or a fanciful compound of 'collie' (dog) and 'shangie'.

definition: Light, frivolous, teasing banter.
exampleSentence: Dinner was all persiflage and laughter, with nothing serious said for hours.
etymology: From French 'persiflage', from 'persifler' (to banter), from 'per-' (intensive) + 'siffler' (to whistle, hiss); mid-18th century.

definition: An informal chat; also a short, light, conversational essay or column.
exampleSentence: His Sunday causerie in the paper read like a friend talking to you over coffee.
etymology: From French 'causer' (to chat), from Latin 'causari'; the essay sense was popularised by Sainte-Beuve's 'Causeries du lundi' (1849).

definition: The ancient Greek virtue of moderation, self-control, and soundness of mind.
exampleSentence: Where others chased excess, she cultivated sophrosyne, wanting only enough.
etymology: From Greek 'sophrosyne', from 'sos' (sound, whole) + 'phren' (mind); a central virtue in Plato's 'Charmides' and in Aristotle.

definition: The perfect, witty retort that comes to you only too late, after the moment has passed.
exampleSentence: Halfway home she was struck by l'esprit de l'escalier — the devastating comeback she should have made an hour ago.
etymology: French, literally 'wit of the staircase'; the image was described by Denis Diderot in 'Paradoxe sur le comédien' (written 1773–78), of thinking of a reply only at the foot of the stairs. The set phrase itself is first attested in French in the 1820s.

definition: The metal cap or band fixed to the end of a tool handle, walking stick, or pencil to strengthen it.
exampleSentence: The rubber ferrule on his cane had worn away, and it clicked on the tiles with every step.
etymology: An alteration (influenced by Latin 'ferrum', iron) of Old French 'virol', from Latin 'viriola' (small bracelet), diminutive of 'viria' (bracelet).

definition: The small plastic or metal sheath at the end of a shoelace.
exampleSentence: The aglet had split, leaving the lace fraying and impossible to thread.
etymology: From Old French 'aiguillette', diminutive of 'aiguille' (needle), from Late Latin 'acucula', diminutive of Latin 'acus' (needle).

definition: The state of being only partly or carelessly dressed.
exampleSentence: She answered the unexpected knock in a state of deshabille, clutching her dressing gown shut.
etymology: From French 'déshabillé' (undressed), past participle of 'déshabiller' (to undress: 'dés-' un- + 'habiller' to dress); late 17th century.

definition: Dreamlike; of or relating to dreams.
exampleSentence: The film had an oneiric quality, its scenes dissolving into one another like half-remembered dreams.
etymology: From Greek 'oneiros' (dream); mid-19th century.

definition: Belonging to the drowsy, hallucinatory state just before falling asleep.
exampleSentence: In that hypnagogic drift she heard her name called, though the house was empty.
etymology: From French 'hypnagogique', from Greek 'hypnos' (sleep) + 'agogos' (leading, inducing); coined by Alfred Maury in the mid-19th century.

definition: Hungry; greedy or voracious.
exampleSentence: The esurient guests eyed the kitchen door long before dinner was announced.
etymology: From Latin 'esurire' (to be hungry), a desiderative of 'edere' (to eat); 17th century.

definition: Very fond of drinking alcohol; also, absorbent of liquid.
exampleSentence: After a bibulous evening at the inn, the poets staggered home reciting verse.
etymology: From Latin 'bibulus', from 'bibere' (to drink); 17th century.

definition: Seized by a violent, compulsive urge to write.
exampleSentence: Scripturient at midnight, she filled three notebooks before the fever passed.
etymology: From Late Latin 'scripturire' (to desire to write), a desiderative of Latin 'scribere' (to write); recorded in English from 1637.

definition: Caring little; nonchalant and indifferent.
exampleSentence: He met the bad news with a pococurante shrug, as though it concerned someone else entirely.
etymology: From Italian 'poco curante' (caring little); from the name of an indifferent Venetian senator in Voltaire's 'Candide' (1759).

definition: Of or relating to the day before yesterday.
exampleSentence: He could recall the nudiustertian dinner in perfect detail but not what he ate this morning.
etymology: From Latin 'nudius tertius', a contraction of 'nunc dies tertius est' (now is the third day); coined by Nathaniel Ward in 'The Simple Cobler of Aggawam' (1647).

definition: Of or belonging to yesterday.
exampleSentence: A faint hesternal sadness lingered, the residue of a quarrel the night before.
etymology: From Latin 'hesternus' (of yesterday) + English '-al'; in English from the late 18th century.

definition: To make a crackling or rattling sound, like a fire or dry leaves underfoot.
exampleSentence: The logs began to crepitate as the flames took hold.
etymology: From Latin 'crepitare' (to crackle), a frequentative of 'crepare' (to creak, crack); 1620s.

definition: To spend the summer in a dormant, torpid state — the hot-weather counterpart of hibernation.
exampleSentence: Buried in the cracked mud, the lungfish estivates until the rains return.
etymology: From Latin 'aestivare' (to spend the summer), from 'aestas' (summer).

definition: To laugh in a smothered, snorting way through the nose while trying to stifle it.
exampleSentence: The pupils snirtled behind their hands as the teacher's chalk snapped a third time.
etymology: Scots, a frequentative of 'snirt' (to snigger, snort); recorded from 1786 in the work of Robert Burns.

definition: To the very last drop; drunk down completely, leaving nothing behind.
exampleSentence: The vintage was so fine they drank it supernaculum, tipping the empty glasses to prove it.
etymology: A mock-Latin rendering of German 'auf den Nagel' (onto the nail), from the old custom of upturning the emptied glass on the thumbnail to prove it was drained; late 16th century.

definition: Of a dark, dusky brownish-grey colour.
exampleSentence: A fuscous moth settled on the windowsill.
etymology: From Latin 'fuscus' (dark, swarthy); first English use 1660s.

definition: The organic compound responsible for the earthy smell of soil and rain.
exampleSentence: That dark, earthy note after the storm is geosmin.
etymology: From Greek 'geo-' (earth) + 'osme' (smell). Coined in 1965 by biochemists Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier at Rutgers, isolating it from Streptomyces.

definition: A state of deep, gloomy absorption or reverie.
exampleSentence: He sat in a brown study, deaf to the conversation.
etymology: From 'brown' in the obsolete sense 'gloomy, dark' + 'study' in the obsolete sense 'reverie'; first attested 1532 (Dice-Play).

definition: A rich, heavy corded silk fabric, or a garment made of it.
exampleSentence: She wore a stiff gown of black paduasoy.
etymology: Alteration of French 'pou-de-soie', influenced by 'Padua say' (a serge from Padua, Italy). OED gives first English use 1663.

definition: A coarse woven woollen fabric or floor-cloth.
exampleSentence: A drugget protected the carpet beneath the dining table.
etymology: From French 'droguet', diminutive of 'drogue'; in English from the late 16th century.

definition: The part of a vocal or instrumental range in which most of a piece lies.
exampleSentence: The aria's high tessitura tires all but the strongest sopranos.
etymology: Italian 'tessitura' (texture, weaving), from 'tessere' (to weave); a doublet of 'texture'.

definition: A run of several notes sung on a single syllable.
exampleSentence: She ended the line on a soaring melisma.
etymology: From Greek 'melisma' (a song, tune), from 'melos' (song); in English from 1837.

definition: A rich, full outpouring of harmonious sound; the principal organ stop.
exampleSentence: The organ's diapason rolled through the nave.
etymology: From Greek 'dia pason (chordon)' (through all the notes); via Latin.

definition: The restless agitation of migratory animals as the season to travel nears.
exampleSentence: The caged warblers fluttered with zugunruhe each autumn.
etymology: German 'Zug' (migration, move) + 'Unruhe' (restlessness); first published 1707, described by ornithologist J. A. Naumann.

definition: Called; named; by the name of.
exampleSentence: A small inn yclept The Green Man stood at the crossroads.
etymology: Middle English, from Old English 'geclypod', past participle of 'clypian' (to call), with the perfective prefix 'y-'.

definition: A small slice or thick cut of meat, especially bacon.
exampleSentence: She fried a collop of bacon for breakfast.
etymology: Late Middle English 'collop', of North Germanic origin; compare Swedish 'kalops' (meat stew).

definition: A large knife; an old word for a knife-fight.
exampleSentence: He drew a wicked snickersnee from his belt.
etymology: Alteration of 'stick or snee', from Dutch 'steken' (to thrust) + 'snijden' (to cut); knife-fight sense 1690s.

definition: To make merry and drink healths; to carouse.
exampleSentence: Villagers wassailed through the orchard on Twelfth Night.
etymology: From Middle English 'wæs hæil', from Old Norse 'ves heill' (be in good health).

definition: Streaks of rain or snow that evaporate before reaching the ground.
exampleSentence: Grey virga trailed beneath the cloud but never wet the field.
etymology: From Latin 'virga' (rod, streak in the sky); meteorological sense from the mid-20th century.

definition: A faint, white arc seen in fog, like a colourless rainbow.
exampleSentence: A pale fogbow arched over the moor at dawn.
etymology: Blend of 'fog' + 'rainbow'; OED's earliest cite is 1820 (William Scoresby).

definition: Mist, fog or steam, especially sea fret rolling off the water.
exampleSentence: A cold roke crept up the estuary by evening.
etymology: Middle English 'roke' (fog, vapour), probably from Old Norse 'roka'; related to 'reek'.

definition: Shining at night; especially of high, tenuous clouds that glow after dusk.
exampleSentence: Noctilucent clouds shimmered silver-blue at midnight.
etymology: From Latin 'nox, noct-' (night) + 'lucent-' (shining), from 'lucere' (to shine); from 1812.

definition: A strong easterly wind of the western Mediterranean.
exampleSentence: A levanter funnelled through the strait, kicking up the swell.
etymology: From 'Levant' (the eastern Mediterranean), from French 'levant' (rising sun, east), from Latin 'levare' (to raise).

definition: An ornamental branched candle-holder, often backed by a mirror.
exampleSentence: A gilt girandole threw candlelight across the ballroom.
etymology: From French 'girandole', from Italian 'girandola', from 'girare' (to turn), from Late Latin 'gyrare'; c.1625–35.

definition: A 'living stone' — a squat succulent disguised as a pebble.
exampleSentence: Her windowsill lithops looked exactly like split grey stones.
etymology: From Greek 'lithos' (stone) + 'ops' (face, appearance); the genus was described from plants found in 1811 by William J. Burchell.

definition: An ancient water clock that measures time by flowing water.
exampleSentence: The orator's speech was timed by a clepsydra.
etymology: From Greek 'klepsydra', from 'kleptein' (to steal) + 'hydor' (water) — literally 'water thief'; in English from 1580.

definition: The branch of meteorology concerned with clouds.
exampleSentence: His nephology notebook named every cloud overhead.
etymology: From Greek 'nephos' (cloud) + '-logy' (study of).

definition: A stupor or trance; a sleeping draught; also deadly nightshade.
exampleSentence: He sank into a dwale and would not be roused.
etymology: Middle English 'dwale' (stupor, deception), from Old English 'dwala' (error), reinforced by Old Norse 'dvala' (sleep); used by Chaucer c.1390.

definition: Proud, splendid, fine or fair.
exampleSentence: The knight rode in armour wlonk and bright.
etymology: From Old English 'wlanc/wlonc' (stately, proud); found in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Pearl.

definition: A soft murmuring, whispering or rustling sound.
exampleSentence: The susurration of the audience died as the lights dimmed.
etymology: From Latin 'susurrare' (to whisper), of imitative origin.

definition: To flirt or have casual love affairs with many people.
exampleSentence: He philandered shamelessly all summer.
etymology: From the obsolete noun 'philander' (a lover), from Greek 'philandros' (loving people/men).

definition: The trance-like ecstasy or rapture that music can induce in listener and performer alike.
exampleSentence: By the third song the whole café had surrendered to tarab, swaying with closed eyes.
etymology: Arabic طرب, from the root ṭ-r-b 'to be moved or delighted'; the merging of musical and emotional enchantment.

definition: An aching homesickness for far-off places you have never even been to.
exampleSentence: A single train timetable was enough to flood him with restless fernweh.
etymology: German, from 'fern' (far) + 'Weh' (woe, ache); literally 'far-sickness', the mirror image of Heimweh (homesickness).

definition: A peace-offering gift brought home to mollify a partner you have annoyed.
exampleSentence: He arrived an hour late clutching tulips and chocolate — unmistakable drachenfutter.
etymology: German, from 'Drache' (dragon) + 'Futter' (fodder); literally 'dragon-fodder', the appeasing offering laid before the beast.

definition: The day after tomorrow, expressed in a single tidy word.
exampleSentence: Not tomorrow, not today — let's settle it on zeg, when the rush is over.
etymology: Georgian ზეგ; part of a full series of day-words including 'mazeg', two days hence. Recorded in Chubinashvili's nineteenth-century Georgian dictionary.

definition: Food packed for a journey but carried back home uneaten, now somehow a small treat.
exampleSentence: The kids begged for the squashed madárlátta sandwiches the moment we got home.
etymology: Hungarian, from the phrase 'a madár látta' — 'the bird saw it'; leftover picnic food the birds glimpsed but no one ate. In Hungarian academic dictionaries.

definition: The giddy disorientation of being far from home in an unfamiliar country.
exampleSentence: The unfamiliar smells and signage filled her with a thrilling dépaysement.
etymology: French, from 'dé-' (un-) + 'pays' (country); the feeling of being 'un-countried', out of one's element.

definition: A truth that everyone knows but, by silent agreement, no one says aloud.
exampleSentence: His drinking was the family mokita, circled around at every dinner but never named.
etymology: Kilivila, of the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea; the truth all agree to leave unspoken.

definition: A frenzy of yearning for something impossible to attain.
exampleSentence: His nympholepsy for a vanished, idealized past kept him from ever living in the present.
etymology: From Greek 'nympholēptos', 'seized by nymphs'; the ancients believed such ecstasy struck those who glimpsed a nymph. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep-rooted sense of honour, dignity and duty toward family and community.
exampleSentence: Out of filotimo the old fisherman refused payment for ferrying the stranded family home.
etymology: Greek φιλότιμο, from 'philos' (love) + 'timi' (honour); literally 'love of honour', a cardinal Greek virtue.

definition: The gentle, bittersweet sadness felt at the fleetingness of all beautiful things.
exampleSentence: Watching the petals scatter, she was filled with mono no aware for the brief spring.
etymology: Japanese 物の哀れ, from 'mono' (things) + 'aware' (pathos); the term was central to the eighteenth-century scholar Motoori Norinaga's literary criticism.

definition: The genuine happiness and satisfaction a person draws from their own work.
exampleSentence: The bakery hummed with an arbejdsglæde you could taste in every loaf.
etymology: Danish, from 'arbejde' (work) + 'glæde' (joy); literally 'work-joy'. Listed in Den Danske Ordbog.

definition: Beautifully understated and austere, with an elegance that deepens with age.
exampleSentence: The worn leather satchel had a shibui charm no new bag could match.
etymology: Japanese 渋い, originally 'astringent' (as of an unripe persimmon); transferred to a quiet, restrained, time-deepened beauty.

definition: Giving confident opinions on matters well beyond one's actual knowledge.
exampleSentence: His ultracrepidarian lectures on medicine annoyed every doctor at the dinner.
etymology: From Latin 'ne ultra crepidam' ('not beyond the sandal'), the painter Apelles' rebuke to a meddling cobbler in Pliny; coined as an English word by William Hazlitt around 1819.

definition: Effortlessly chic and refined, with a worldly stylishness that never tries too hard.
exampleSentence: Her plain grey coat and single pin were unmistakably iki.
etymology: Japanese 粋; the Edo-period merchant-class aesthetic analysed in Kuki Shūzō's 1930 treatise 'The Structure of Iki' as a blend of coquetry, composure and resignation.

definition: Boldly self-confident, cheeky and a little flashily daring.
exampleSentence: The wee one strode onstage gallus as you like and belted the first note.
etymology: Scots, possibly from 'gallows' (one fit for the gallows, hence reckless); now an admiring word for swagger. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Habitually gloomy, taciturn and darkly sardonic in temperament.
